About this citation

The Analects is a compiled record of sayings, not a work by Confucius. The common formula 'Confucius said' refers to a tradent whose words were assembled by later hands, and the book-and-chapter locator is what makes a passage findable in any edition.

Reading the cited source

The archive attributes this English wording to Analects 15.21 and files it under Confucianism.

What a locator tells you, and what it does not · How this archive traces a quotation

About Confucius

Confucius (Kong Qiu, 551–479 BCE) taught in the late Spring and Autumn period amid the Zhou order’s political fragmentation. Born in the state of Lu, he briefly held local office and then spent years seeking rulers who would adopt ritual-based, virtue-centered government.

Interpretation

Confucius is drawing a contrast about where the cause is located. The exemplary person looks to themselves when something fails; the petty person looks to others. The claim is not that others are never at fault but that the location of the search determines whether anything can be done about it. In the Analects this is one of several passages making self-direction the mark of the person worth emulating.

Why it matters

It is a reliable diagnostic in practice: notice where you look first when something goes wrong. That reflex determines what you can do next.

Questions readers arrive with

What is the source of the quotation “The Master said: The gentleman seeks it in…”?

“The Master said: The gentleman seeks it in…” comes from The Analects, 15.21 (c. 5th–3rd century BCE (compiled)), attributed to Confucius.

What does Confucius mean by responsibility?

Philosophical debates cover free will, blame, collective responsibility, and duties to distant others. Technology and AI revive the question of who is accountable when systems act. This passage enters that discussion through responsibility.
